lines: Title: Subset Sum in Near-Linear Pseudopolynomial Time and Polynomial Space
\title{Subset Sum in Near-Linear Pseudopolynomial Time and Polynomial Space}

Given a multiset $A = \{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ of positive integers and a target integer $t$, the \textsc{SubsetSum} problem asks if there is a subset of $A$ that sums to $t$. Bellman's [1957] classical dynamic programming algorithm runs in $O(nt)$ time and $O(t)$ space. Since then, there have been multiple improvements in both time and space complexity.

Notably, Bringmann [SODA 2017] uses a two-step color-coding technique to obtain a randomized algorithm that runs in $\tilde{O}(n+t)$ time and $\tilde{O}(t)$ space. On the other hand, there are polynomial space algorithms -- for example, Jin, Vyas and Williams [SODA 2021] build upon the algorithm given by Bringmann, using a clever algebraic trick first seen in Kane's Logspace algorithm, to obtain an $\tilde{O}(nt)$ time and $\tilde{O}(\log(nt))$ space algorithm. A natural question, asked by Jin et al. is if there is an $\tilde{O}(n+t)$ time algorithm running in poly$(n, \log t)$ space. Another natural question is whether it is possible to construct a deterministic polynomial space algorithm with time complexity comparable to that of Bellman's.

In this paper, we answer both questions affirmatively. We build on the framework given by Jin et al., using a multipoint evaluation-based approach to speed up a bottleneck step in their algorithm. We construct:
\item a deterministic algorithm that runs in $\tilde{O}(nt)$ time and $\tilde{O}(n \log^2 t)$ space
\item a randomized algorithm that runs in $\tilde{O}(n+t)$ time and $\tilde{O}(n^2 + n \log^2 t)$ space.

Given a (multi-)set $A = \{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ of positive integers and a target integer $t$, the \textsc{SubsetSum} problem asks if there is a subset of $A$ that sums to $t$. Bellman's classical dynamic programming algorithm runs in $O(nt)$ time and $O(t)$ space. We work in the word-RAM model with word length $\Theta(\log n + \log t)$, and so the algorithms in this paper run in \textit{pseudopolynomial} time.

Since Bellman gave his textbook algorithm in 1957, many results improving the time complexity have been published. Koiliaris and Xu \cite{koiliaris2019faster} construct a $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n}t)$ time deterministic algorithm. Bringmann \cite{bringmann2017near} uses a two-step color-coding technique to obtain a randomized algorithm that runs in $\tilde{O}(n+t)$ time and $\tilde{O}(t)$ space\footnote{$\tilde{O}(T)$ denotes an upper bound omitting $\polylog T$ factors.}.

Interestingly, \textsc{SubsetSum} has pseudopolynomial time algorithms that also run in polynomial space. Such low-space algorithms are interesting, since space is often a scarcer resource than time for many applications. Lokshtanov and Nederlof \cite{lokshtanov2010saving} present an algorithm that uses Fast Fourier Transforms running in $\tilde{O}(n^3t)$ time and $O(n^2)$ space. Bringmann \cite{bringmann2017near} presents a randomized algorithm dependent on the \textit{Extended Riemann Hypothesis}, running in time $\tilde{O}(nt)$ and space $O(n \log t)$, building on top of Lokshtanov and Nederlof's work.

On the other hand, there are polynomial space algorithms that leverage an algebraic trick first seen in Kane's Logspace algorithm \cite{kane2010unary}. Recently, Jin, Vyas and Williams \cite{jin2021fast} cleverly combined Kane's approach with Bringmann's linear-time algorithm to obtain an algorithm running in $\tilde{O}(nt)$ time and $\tilde{O}(\log(nt))$ space.
This leads us to two natural open questions, the first of which was explicitly posed by Jin et al. \cite{jin2021fast}:
\item Does there exist a $\tilde{O}(n+t)$-time, poly$(n, \log t)$-space algorithm for \textsc{SubsetSum}?
\item Does there exist a deterministic polynomial space algorithm for \textsc{SubsetSum} with runtime comparable to that of Bellman's algorithm?

The first question is especially compelling, since a runtime of $\tilde{O}(n+t)$ is provably near-optimal in terms of $t$. This follows from the lower-bound established by Abboud, Bringmann, Hermelin and Shabtay \cite{abboud2022seth} based on the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH), that rules out algorithms with a runtime of $O(2^{o(n)}t^{1-\varepsilon})$, for fixed $\varepsilon > 0$. This suggests that an algorithm achieving both a near-optimal runtime and polynomial space would be quite surprising.

\textbf{Our Results.} In this paper, we answer both questions affirmatively. We build on the framework given by Jin et al., using a multipoint evaluation-based approach to speed up a bottleneck step in their algorithm. We construct:
\item a deterministic algorithm that runs in $\tilde{O}(nt)$ time and $\tilde{O}(n \log^2 t)$ space
\item a randomized algorithm that runs in $\tilde{O}(n+t)$ time and $\tilde{O}(n^2 + n \log^2 t)$ space.

Consider the polynomial $A(x) = \prod_{i=1}^n (1+x^{a_{i}})$ associated with the \textsc{SubsetSum} instance $(A = \{a_1, \cdots, a_n\}, t)$. Expanding the polynomial out, we see that the coefficient of $x^t$ is nonzero precisely when $t$ is a subsum of $A$. The following trick, first seen in \cite{kane2010unary} can be used to check if the coefficient of $x^t$ is nonzero.

\textnormal{\cite{kane2010unary}} Let $\mathbb{F}_p$ be the finite field of order $p$, for some prime $p$. Given an integer polynomial $f(x)$ of degree $d$ less than $p$, and $0 < t \leq d$, define $c_t$ to be the coefficient of $x^t$. Then: \[-c_t \bmod p = \sum_{x \in \mathbb{F}_p^*} x^{p - 1 - t} f(x).\]
Thus, the sum is zero if and only if $p \mid c_t$.
Let $g$ be a generator for the cyclic group $\mathbb{F}_p^{*}$. Consider the following sum, for some integer $a$:
Then, if $f(x) = \sum_{i=0}^{d}c_i x^i$, we have: \[\sum_{x \in \mathbb{F}_p^*} x^{p - 1 - t} f(x) = \sum_{x \in \mathbb{F}_p^*} x^{p - 1 - t} \left(\sum_{i=0}^{d}c_j x^j\right) = -c_t \bmod p\]

Such computations can be done in low-space and are thus especially useful in this context. Both of our low-space algorithms have a similar high-level structure: choose a `large enough' prime $q$, an appropriate polynomial $p(x)$ encoding the \textsc{SubsetSum} instance, and compute the sum described above to extract the required coefficient. Instead of computing the sum term-by-term, we may employ the following technique:

\textnormal{(Multipoint Evaluation)} Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Given a polynomial $f(x) \in R[x]$ of degree $d = O(n)$, where $n = 2^k$, and evaluation points $u_0, \cdots, u_{n-1}$, one can compute $f(u_0), \cdots, f(u_{n-1})$ in $O(n \polylog n)$ time and space.
(Sketch, see \cite{vonZurGathen2013}, Section 10.1 for a more detailed proof.)
\] for $0 \leq i \leq k$, $0 \leq j \leq 2^{k-i}-1$. Doing this carefully, as shown in the reference, takes $\tilde{O}(n)$ time and space.

Then, compute $f_0(x) = f(x) \bmod (x-u_0)\cdots(x-u_{n/2-1})$ and $f_1(x) = f(x) \bmod (x-u_{n/2})\cdots(x-u_{n-1})$. Notice that $f$ agrees with $f_0$ and $f_1$ on the first and last $n/2$ points respectively. We can now recurse, asking for $\{f_0(u_0), \cdots, f_0(u_{n/2})\}$ and $\{f_1(u_{n/2+1}), \cdots, f_1(u_{n-1})\}$. Notice that the polynomials that appear as dividends in the recursion are precisely the polynomials $M_{i, j}$ computed earlier. Note that $f_0$ and $f_1$ have degree at most $n/2$.

We obtain the following recurrence for the time complexity: \[T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(D(n))\] where $D(n)$ is the time taken to perform the divisions. Since $D(n) = O(n \polylog n)$, we have $T(n) = O(n \polylog n)$, as well.

There are two obstacles to applying multipoint evaluation directly. First, the polynomials that we consider have degree $\Omega(t)$, and thus storing the polynomials $M_{i, j}$ takes too much space. Second, computing remainders usually requires FFT, which again takes $\Omega(t)$ space. However, by ordering the evaluation points carefully, one can avoid the pre-computation step and compute remainders quickly and in low-space. The following lemma will help us do so.

Let $q$ be a prime power, and write $q-1 = 2^kr$, where $r$ is odd. Let $g$ be a generator of $\mathbb{F}_q^{*}$ and define the coset $H = g^{s+j}\langle \left(g^{r}\right)^{2^i} \rangle$, where $0 \leq s < r$, $0 \leq j < 2^i$ and $0 \leq i < k$.  Then, the polynomial $p_H(x)$ defined as

The degrees of the polynomials on the LHS and the RHS match, since $|H| = 2^{k-i}$. It then suffices to check that for each $h \in H$, $h^{2^{k-i}} = \left(g^{s+j}\right)^{2^{k-i}}$, which holds since each element of $\left(g^{-(s+j)}\right)H$ has order dividing $2^{k-i}$.
When we order the points using the above lemma, we shall see that it becomes natural to minimize $r$. The following result will prove useful:
Let $a$ and $d$ be coprime integers. Define $\pi(x; d, a)$ to be the number of primes less than $x$ that are congruent to $a \pmod{d}$. Then:
\pi(x; d, a) = \frac{1}{\phi(d)} \cdot \frac{x}{\ln x} + E(x; a, d),
where $E(x; a, d)$ is an error term satisfying $E(x; a, d) = o(\pi(x; d, a))$. Here, $\phi$ denotes Euler's totient function.
A polynomial $f(x)$ is called \textbf{n-sparse} if at most n of its coefficients are nonzero.

A polynomial $f(x)$ is called \textbf{$\Pi$-n-sparse} it can be written as a product $f(x) = f_1(x) \cdots f_l(x)$, where each $f_i(x)$ is $k_i$-sparse, and $k_1 + \cdots +k_l \leq n$. We call such a factorization a \textbf{presentation} of $f$.

We may analogously define polynomials that are $\Sigma\Pi$-n-sparse or $\Pi\Sigma\Pi$-n-sparse. Such polynomials of degree at most $d$ can be stored in $O(n \log d)$ space, provided that each coefficient in each presentation polynomial is $\tilde{O}(d)$. This is because storing each coefficient-exponent pair takes $O(\log d)$ space, and at most $n$ such pairs need to be stored.

\textbf{Remark.} Suppose that we have a $\Pi$-n-sparse polynomial $p(x)$ with presentation $p_1(x)\cdots p_l(x)$ and we need to compute $p(x) \bmod p_H(x)$ for some coset $H$ as described above. Instead of computing the remainder using a standard method, we use the sparsity of $p(x)$ and the fact that $p_H(x)$ only has two terms, and replace each monomial $x^a$ in each $p_i(x)$ by its image modulo $p_H(x)$, which is itself a monomial. Computing a remainder polynomial as such takes $O(n \log d)$ time and space. Similar arguments hold for $\Sigma\Pi$-n-sparse or $\Pi\Sigma\Pi$-n-sparse polynomials. \textit{All remainders in both algorithms are computed as described above.}\\
We use the techniques described above to obtain the following theorems:
There is a deterministic $\tilde{O}(nt)$ time, $\tilde{O}(n \log ^2 t)$ space algorithm for \textsc{SubsetSum}.
There is a randomized $\tilde{O}(n + t)$ time, $\tilde{O}(n^2+n \log ^2 t)$ space algorithm for \textsc{SubsetSum}.

The algorithm in Theorem~\ref{thm:rand} is Monte Carlo with one-sided error, in that it returns YES on a valid instance with probability $1-\frac{1}{\Omega(n+t)}$, and always returns NO on an invalid instance.
We prove Theorem~\ref{thm:det}, providing a simple deterministic algorithm. The novel ideas carry over neatly to the randomized algorithm.

We start by looking at the polynomial $A(x) = (1+x^{a_1})\cdots(1+x^{a_n})$. Note that this polynomial is $\Pi$-$O(n)$-sparse, and that when expanded, each coefficient in the polynomial is bounded from above by $nt$.
There is a prime $q \in (nt, nt \log nt]$, such that $q-1 = 2^k r$, where $r$ is odd and at most $q^{1/2}$.

Let $2^k$ be the smallest power of two larger than $(nt \log nt)^{1/2}$. We then estimate the number of primes that are 1 ($\bmod \;2^k$) and lie in the range $(nt, nt \log nt]$ using the theorem stated above. We have, for large enough $n$ and $t$:
\pi(nt \log nt; 2^k, 1) - \pi(nt; 2^k, 1) &= \frac{1}{2^{k-1}}\left[\frac{nt \log nt}{\log (nt \log nt)} - \frac{nt}{\log nt}\right] + E\left(nt\log nt, 2^k, 1\right) - E\left(nt, 2^k, 1\right)\\

where the first inequality follows from the fact that $E(x; a, d) = o(\pi(x; d, a))$, and the remaining follow from simple bounding. Thus, there is a prime of the form $r\cdot2^k + 1$ in the interval $(nt, nt \log nt]$, where $r \le (nt \log nt)^{1/2} \le 2^k$. Thus, $q-1 = 2^k r \ge r^2$, giving us a prime with the required bound.

We may run through the interval $(nt, nt \log nt]$ and find such a prime in $\tilde{O}(nt)$ time and $\tilde{O}(\polylog nt)$ space deterministically. Simply check each number in the range for primality using the AKS primality test \cite{agrawal2004primes}, and for each prime, successively divide by two to obtain the corresponding value of $r$, and accept if $r < q^{1/2}$. Upon obtaining such a prime $q$, a generator $g$ for $\mathbb{F}_q^{*}$ can be found in $\tilde{O}(nt)$ time and $\tilde{O}(\polylog nt)$ space, simply by iterating through each element of the group and using binary exponentiation to find the order. Write $q-1 = 2^kr$, as above. Note that $q = \tilde{\Theta}(nt)$ We now assume that $n \leq t$; otherwise, we may use Bellman's textbook (deterministic) algorithm that now runs in $\tilde{O}(nt)$ time and $\tilde{O}(t) = \tilde{O}(n)$ space.

Consider the polynomial $f(x) = A(x) x^{q-1-t}$, having degree $d = \tilde{\Theta}(nt)$. Note that the coefficient $c_t$ of $x^t$ in $A(x)$ can be bounded as such: $c_t \leq nt < q$. Thus, $c_t = 0$ if and only if $\sum_{x \in \mathbb{F}_q^*} f(x) = 0$. Let $\langle g \rangle$ be the multiplicative group of the field and $l = \left\lfloor \log n \right\rfloor$.

We may now use Lemma~\ref{lem:algtrick} to isolate the required coefficient, using multipoint evaluation to compute the sum quickly. The obstacles discussed earlier are no longer relevant, since precomputation is not required at all, and we may compute remainders without using FFT, since $f(x)$ is $\Pi$-$\tilde{O}(n)$-sparse. As we shall see in the algorithm, using the sparsity allows us to compute remainders in $\tilde{O}(n \log d)$ time. This offers a speed-up for the first $k-l$ levels. However, in the last $l$ levels, the polynomials have degree $\tilde{O}(n)$, and it is thus better to compute the remainders in the last $l$ levels using the standard FFT-based method.
Consider the following algorithm that computes the required sum: \\
\KwIn{Polynomial $f(x)$, multiplicative group of the field $\langle g \rangle$}
Compute the required sum using standard multipoint evaluation\;
The algorithm \textsc{FastSumComputation}($f(x)$, $\langle g \rangle$) returns $\sum_{x \in \langle g \rangle} f(x)$.

The proof follows from an argument similar to that of the proof of the multipoint evaluation lemma. The only major difference is that we first divide the evaluation into $r$ batches, instead of the usual binary split. It thus suffices to show the correctness of \textsc{FastBinaryCosetSum} on each batch.

We show the correctness of \textsc{FastBinaryCosetSum}($p(x)$, $g^{s+j}\langle \left(g^{r}\right)^{2^{i}} \rangle$, $\texttt{currentSum}$) inductively. When $i = k-l$, the correctness follows from that of the multipoint evaluation lemma. For the inductive step, assume correctness for smaller values of $i$. Observe that $H \sqcup K = g^{s+j}\langle \left(g^{r}\right)^{2^{i}} \rangle$, and that $p(x)$ and $p_0(x)$ agree on $H$ while $p(x)$ and $p_1(x)$ agree on $K$. It follows that the sum over $g^{s+j}\langle \left(g^{r}\right)^{2^{i}} \rangle$ is correct as well.
The algorithm \textsc{FastSumComputation}($f(x)$, $\langle g \rangle$) runs in $\tilde{O}(nt)$ time.
We split the sum into $r$ batches, and computing the remainder polynomial $f_H$ for each batch takes $O(n \log d)$ time, giving a total runtime of $O(nr \log d)$.

For a particular batch, the time taken to compute \textsc{FastBinaryCosetSum}($f_H(x)$, $g^s \langle g^r \rangle$, \texttt{sum}) can be computed by looking at the corresponding recursion tree. The (binary) tree has depth $k-l$ and so has $O(2^k/n)$ nodes. Each leaf corresponds to a standard instance of multipoint evaluation on $n$ points, and thus the time taken at each leaf is $O(n \polylog n)$. At each internal node, we spend $O(n \log d)$ time computing the two remainder polynomials. Thus, the total time taken is: $O(\frac{2^k}{n}\cdot n\log d + \frac{2^k}{n}\cdot n\polylog n) = O(2^k (\log d + \polylog n))$.

Thus, the time taken across all batches is: $O(nr \log d + 2^k (\log d + \polylog n) r) = O(nr \log d + q (\log d + \polylog n))$. Combined with the fact that $r < q^{1/2}$ and $q = \tilde{\Theta}(d)$, the runtime is $\tilde{O}(nd^{1/2} + d)$. Since $d = \tilde{\Theta}(nt)$ and $n \leq t$, the final runtime is $\tilde{O}(n^{3/2}t^{1/2}+nt) = \tilde{O}(nt)$.
The algorithm \textsc{FastSumComputation}($f(x)$, $\langle g \rangle$) runs in $\tilde{O}(n \log^2 t)$ space.

We shall find the space used by FastBinaryCosetSum using induction. At depth $k-l$ in the recursion tree, computing the sum using standard multipoint evaluation takes $O(n \polylog n)$ space. Assume that at depth $i+1$, the space used is $O((k-l-i-1) n \log q + n \polylog n)$. At depth $i$, the space used by FastBinaryCosetSum($p(x)$, $g^{s+j}\langle \left(g^{r}\right)^{2^{i}} \rangle$, $\texttt{currentSum}$) is $O(n \log q + (k-l-i-1) n \log q + n \polylog n) = O((k-l-i) n \log q + n \polylog n)$, where the the first term comes from storing the remainder polynomials and the second term comes from the space used by the recursive calls made. We may reuse the space used by each recursive call. Thus, FastBinaryCosetSum($f_H(x)$, $g^s \langle g^r \rangle$, \texttt{sum}) takes $O(n \polylog n + (k-l) n \log q) = O(n \polylog n + n \log^2 q)$ space.

We split the computation in FastSumComputation($f(x)$, $\langle g \rangle$) into $r$ batches. We then use FastBinaryCosetSum on each batch. The space can be reused for each batch. Thus, the space taken is $O(n \polylog n + n \log^2 q) = \tilde{O}(n \log ^2 d) = \tilde{O}(n \log ^2t)$, as required.

We may compute the required sum using the algorithm given above in the case $n \leq t$, giving us a final algorithm for \textsc{SubsetSum} that runs in $\tilde{O}(nt)$ time and $\tilde{O}(n \log ^2t)$ space.

\textbf{Note.} We may use \textsc{FastSumComputation} to compute the sum $\sum_{x \in \mathbb{F_q^{*}} f(x)}$ for a general $\Pi$-$\tilde{O}(n)$-sparse (or $\Pi\Sigma\Pi$-$\tilde{O}(n)$-sparse) polynomial $f(x)$ with degree $d = \tilde{\Theta}(q)$ and coefficients bounded by $O(\log d)$ in time $\tilde{O}(nd^{1/2} + d)$ and space $\tilde{O}(n \log ^2 d)$.

We use the techniques developed in the previous section, along with a clever two-step color-coding-based construction seen first in \cite{bringmann2017near} and later refined in \cite{jin2021fast}, to prove Theorem~\ref{thm:rand}. We sketch the construction given in \cite{jin2021fast} below.
There exists a randomized algorithm that, on input a \textsc{SubsetSum} instance $(A, t)$, returns a polynomial $\tilde{A}(x)$ of degree at most $2t \log^3 n$, such that:
\item If $t$ is a valid target, the coefficient of $x^t$ in $\tilde{A}(x)$ is nonzero with probability $1 - \frac{1}{\Omega(n + t)}$;
\item If $t$ is not a valid target, then the coefficient is zero with probability $1$.
Furthermore, the polynomial $\tilde{A}(x)$ can be computed in $O(n \polylog t)$ time and $\tilde{O}(n \log t)$ space.
(Very rough sketch, the construction is explained in greater detail in the \hyperref[sec:app]{Appendix})

The idea is to construct the polynomial $A(x)$ and \textit{collapse} certain terms in the product randomly. Suppose $t$ is a valid target and $R$ is a subset of $A$ that sums to $t$. Call the elements of $R$ \textit{relevant}. The idea is to partition $A$ randomly, ensuring with high probability that no two relevant elements end up in the same partition. Suppose such a partition is $A = \bigsqcup_{i} T_i$. We may then construct the polynomial $\tilde{A}(x) = \prod_{i}(1+\sum_{a \in T_i} x^a)$. Note that the coefficient of $x^t$ is nonzero with high probability, since it is unlikely that any two relevant items lie in the same $T_i$. Note that such partitions cannot give us false positives, since we only limit the possible subsums by partitioning.

In particular, it is important to note that the polynomial $\tilde{A}(x)$ is $\Pi\Sigma\Pi$-$\tilde{O}(n)$-sparse and has a presentation in which each monomial has coefficients from $\{ 0, 1 \}$. Expanding the polynomial out, we see that the coefficients are $\tilde{O}(t)$.

We define $d = 2t \log^3 n$, and let $c_t$ denote the coefficient of $x^t$ in $\tilde{A}(x)$. Note that $c_t$ is at most the number of subsets of $A$ that add to $t$, which in turn is at most $2^n$. Then, the number of primes larger than $d$ that divide $c_t$ is bounded from above by $\frac{n}{\log d}$.

We may assume that $n \le \frac{1}{3} \sqrt{d/\log d}$; otherwise, we may use the near-linear time algorithm given by Bringmann \cite{bringmann2017near}, which now runs in $\tilde{O}(n+t)$ time and $\tilde{O}(t) = \tilde{O}(n^{2})$ space.
There are at least $3n/\log d$ primes $q \in (d, d \log d]$, such that $q - 1 = 2^k r$, where $r < q^{1/2}$ and $r$ is odd.

Let $2^k$ be the smallest power of two larger than $(d \log d)^{1/2}$. We shall now estimate the number of primes that are 1 ($\bmod \;2^k$) and lie in the range $(d, d \log d]$, again using the theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions.
\pi(d \log d; 2^k, 1) - \pi(d; 2^k, 1) &= \frac{1}{2^{k-1}}\left[\frac{d \log d}{\log (d \log d)} - \frac{d}{\log d}\right] + E\left(d\log d, 2^k, 1\right) - E\left(d, 2^k, 1\right)\\

where the first inequality again follows from $E(x; d, a) = o(\pi(x; d, a))$ and the third from the fact that $n \le \frac{1}{3} \sqrt{d/\log d}$. Then, if $q$ is such a prime, we may write $q-1 = 2^k r$, where $r \le \frac{q}{2^k} \le q^{1/2}$.
\KwOut{\texttt{True} if there exists a subset summing to $t$, \texttt{False} otherwise}
Run Bringmann's near-linear time algorithm and\\
Compute the set of primes described above;\\
Choose a prime $q$ uniformly at random from this set and compute a generator $g$ of $\mathbb{F}_q^{*}$;\\
Repeat the last two steps $\log (n+t)$ times;\\

Suppose $t$ is a valid target. For \textsc{LinearLowSpaceSubsetSum}($A$, $t$) to fail, we need every chosen prime $q$ to divide $c_t$, which happens with probability $(\frac{2}{3})^{\log (n+t)} = \frac{1}{\Omega(n+t)}$, or for $c_t$ to be zero, which happens with probability $\frac{1}{\Omega(n+t)}$. The union bound tells us that the final error probability is $1 - \frac{1}{\Omega(n+t)}$.
On the other hand, the algorithm is always correct when $t$ is not a valid target, since the sum computed is always zero.
The algorithm \textsc{LinearLowSpaceSubsetSum}($A$, $t$) runs in $\tilde{O}(n + t)$ time and $\tilde{O}(n^2 + n \log^2 t)$ space.

Computing the polynomial $\tilde{A}(x)$ takes $O(n \polylog t)$ time and $\tilde{O}(n \log t)$ space. As before, we use the AKS primality test to find the primes of the required form in near-linear time and low space. Since the polynomial $\tilde{A}(x)x^{q-1-t}$ is $\Pi\Sigma\Pi$-$\tilde{O}(n)$-sparse, and has $\tilde{O}(t)$ coefficients, an argument similar to the one given previously shows us that FastSumComputation($\tilde{A}(x)x^{q-1-t}, \langle g \rangle)$ runs in $O(n \polylog t + nd^{1/2} + d)$ time and $O(n \polylog n + n \log^2 d)$ space. Now using the fact that $n = \tilde{O}(d^{1/2})$, we have that the run time is $O(n + t)$ and the space used is $O(n \log^2 q)$. Combining this with the case where $n = \Omega(d^{1/2})$, the final runtime is $O(n + t)$ and the space used is $O(n^2 + n \log^2 q)$.

In this paper, we presented two new algorithms for \textsc{SubsetSum} that speed up previous low-space approaches. We presented a deterministic algorithm that runs in $\tilde{O}(nt)$ time and $\tilde{O}(n \log ^2 t)$ space along with a near-linear $\tilde{O}(n+t)$ time randomized algorithm that uses only $\tilde{O}(n^2 + n \log ^2 t)$ space. Our key contribution was to use a divide-and-conquer approach to speed up the computation of the sum of a polynomial over the multiplicative group of a finite field. An important point is that our contributions do not use randomness at all. Any algorithm for \textsc{SubsetSum} that uses Kane's summation trick can be sped up using the techniques shown here.

We conclude with some open problems. Jin et al. present an algorithm running in $\tilde{O}(nt)$ time $O(\log nt)$ space. Is there a time-space tradeoff algorithm that interpolates between their algorithm and the $\tilde{O}(n+t)$ time $\tilde{O}(n^2 + n \log t)$ space randomized algorithm presented here? Is there a way to construct a deterministic polynomial space algorithm that runs in $O(\sqrt n t)$ time, giving a polynomial space variant of the algorithm given in Koiliaris \& Xu \cite{koiliaris2019faster}? Can the space used by the randomized algorithm given in Theorem~\ref{thm:rand} be improved to $O(\log (nt))$?
I am grateful to Professor V. Arvind for introducing me to the paper by Jin et al. and for his patient guidance and constructive discussions throughout the summer.
We summarize the construction of the polynomial in Lemma~\ref{lem:poly}, taken from \cite{jin2021fast}. They first construct a hash family with the following properties:

There is an \textbf{efficiently invertible} hash family $\mathcal{H} = \{h: [n] \xrightarrow{} [m]\}$, for all $0 \leq m \leq n$, with the following \textbf{load-balancing} property: given a set $S \subset [n], |S| = m$, with high probability, $|S \cap h^{-1}(\{i\})| \leq C \log n$, for each $1 \le i \le m$ and some $C > 0$ depending only on $\mathcal{H}$, where $h$ is chosen uniformly at random from the hash family. A hash function can be specified using a seed of length $\tilde{O}(\log n)$.
Intuitively, the hash family distributes each subset of size $m$ over the image with very few collisions. We now give the algorithm to construct the polynomial:
\textbf{Layer Splitting:} Split the multiset $A$ into $\left\lceil \log n \right\rceil$ layers as such:  $
L_i = (t/2^i,\, t/2^{i-1}] \cap A$, $\forall\, 1 \leq i \leq \lceil \log n \rceil - 1$ and $L_{\lceil \log n \rceil} = A \setminus \left(L_1 \cup \cdots \cup L_{\lceil \log n \rceil - 1}\right)$.

\textbf{Two-Layer Partition:} Call a subset $R$ of $A$ \textit{relevant} if the sum of the elements in $R$ is $t$. Note that the \(i\)th layer contains at most $2^i$ relevant elements. We now split this layer using a random hash function $h : [|L_i|] \xrightarrow{} [2^i]$ from the hash family shown above. Thus, we partition $L_i = S_1 \sqcup S_2 \cdots \sqcup S_{2^i}$, and the load-balancing property tells us that each $S_j$ contains at most $O(\log n)$ relevant elements. We extract each $S_j$ using the \textit{efficient invertibilty} of the hash family. Let $r = \left\lceil \log n \right\rceil$. We now partition each $S_j$ into $r^2$ disjoint sets $T_1, \cdots, T_{r^2}$ by placing each element of $S_j$ into a set $T_i$, where $i$ is chosen uniformly at random. A simple counting argument shows that the relevant elements in $S_j$ all go into different sets in the partition with probability at least $3/4$.

Thus, the polynomial $\prod_{i = 1}^{r^2}(1+\sum_{a \in T_i}x^a)$ contains the monomial $x^c$, where $c$ is the sum of the relevant items in $S_j$, with probability at least $3/4$. We repeat this last step $\Theta(r)$ times and add all the polynomials up. This gives a polynomial of the form $\sum_{\Theta(r)}\prod_{i = 1}^{r^2}(1+\sum_{a \in T_i}x^a)$, that contains the monomial $x^c$ with probability at least $1 - 1/n^{O(1)}$. Such a procedure associates a polynomial with each $S_j$. We now multiply all such polynomials together, giving us a polynomial $\tilde{A}(x) = \prod_{L_i}\prod_{j}\sum_{r}\prod_{i = 1}^{r^2}(1+\sum_{a \in T_i}x^a)$.

A careful argument shows that this polynomial contains a monomial of the form $x^t$ with probability $1-1/n^{O(1)}$, if $t$ is a valid target. Note that such a polynomial can only contain monomials with exponents corresponding to subsums. Thus, if $t$ is not a valid target, the polynomial shown above will not contain the monomial $x^t$.

It can be shown that the algorithm described above can be implemented in $O(n \polylog t)$ time and $\tilde{O}(n \log t)$ space. Note that each element of the set $A$ can appear as an exponent in $\tilde{A}(x)$ at most $O(\log n)$ times (this happens because of the repetition done to boost the probability from $3/4$ to $1-1/n$). This shows us that the polynomial constructed is $\Pi\Sigma\Pi$-$\tilde{O}(n)$-sparse. Bounding the degree gives us that the polynomial $\tilde{A}(x)$ has degree at most $2 (\log ^3 n) \max A \leq 2 (\log ^3 n) t$.
